summary: Describes the conventions to be followed by those who run networks and hosts on the Internet, summarizing the unwritten oral tradition on the subject. It is one author's view and informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The unwritten rules of being a good Internet neighbor, finally written down.

questions: responsibilities of host and network managers
how do you handle internet problems
subtitle: Unwritten rules for keeping the Internet running

tldr.problem: The Internet is decentralized with no central authority, so it depends on people running networks and servers to follow shared practices. The unwritten conventions had never been formally documented.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1173 codifies the oral tradition: network managers must be reachable and accountable, host managers must be accessible, every mail server must have a postmaster, and all must cooperate to solve problems spanning multiple sites.
tldr.outcome: This document serves as a reference for what responsible Internet operations look like, balancing management authority with community cooperation.

today: RFC 1173 is Informational, documenting community norms as of August 1990. These principles remain central to Internet operations today, though many networks now have formal service level agreements and incident response procedures in addition to these basic expectations.

sections.title: Basic Responsibilities
sections.content:
The Internet is a cooperative endeavor. Its usefulness depends on reasonable behavior from every user, host and router. People in charge of networks and systems must be aware of their responsibilities and attentive to local conditions.

The key requirement: those responsible for networks and hosts must be accessible via both email and telephone, and responsive to problem reports from other parts of the Internet. Even small local problems like a crash or power failure can have widespread effects elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot just run a server and ignore it. You have to answer when someone from another network calls with a problem.

sections.title: Network and Host Managers
sections.content:
Every IP network or subnet must have a responsible manager. That person must supply their name, phone number and address to the Internet NIC, and must have either direct system access to every host on the network, or the authority to power off or physically disconnect systems that misbehave.

Network managers for high-traffic networks should be reachable 24 hours a day. Every host must have a responsible manager with authority to configure and control access. Critical systems like mail relays must have managers available 24/7.

Every host that handles mail beyond the local network must maintain a mailbox named postmaster, read regularly by a system maintainer. This is the contact point for mail delivery problems and security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone has to be in charge of each network and each important computer. Their phone number must be published. They answer when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Problem Classes and Responses
sections.content:
The RFC categorizes problems into three classes. User-related problems (bouncing mail, misbehavior on mailing lists, security violations) usually need education or enforcement. Host-related problems (misconfiguration, buggy software, security holes) may need reconfiguration or vendor involvement. Network-related problems (routing errors, loops, topology issues) may require escalation up to the level of cutting off an offending network.

Each class needs different handling, but all require communication and cooperation between the affected sites.
sections.plainLanguage: When things break, managers have to figure out whose problem it is and work together to fix it.

sections.title: Security and Shared Responsibility
sections.content:
The Internet is not secure by design. Managers must understand that they cannot fully protect their systems against external attacks. Security depends on the cooperation of all responsible individuals to share information about threats and patch vulnerabilities.

At the same time, each manager is ultimately responsible for their own security. Those running sensitive systems must be intimately familiar with their operating system and network software.
sections.plainLanguage: No one can lock down the Internet completely, but everyone has to help by fixing their own problems and telling others about threats.
